title: Two Sum
interviewTips: Always clarify whether the input array can contain negative numbers, duplicate numbers, or if multiple valid pairs exist.
State why the brute-force nested loop is quadratic before leaping into the hash map to demonstrate problem-solving progression.
Mention that returning indices means sorting would require storing pairs (value, index), which takes O(N) space anyway.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force (Nested Loops)
approaches.intuition: Check every possible pair of elements in the array to see if their sum matches the target. This simulates what a human would do by testing each number against every other subsequent number.
approaches.theory: For an array of length N, there are N * (N - 1) / 2 unique pairs. By running two nested loops—outer index i from 0 to N-1 and inner index j from i+1 to N-1—we evaluate every combination without evaluating duplicate pairs or an element with itself.

timeComplexity.explanation: Two nested loops inspecting N * (N - 1) / 2 pairs in the worst case.

spaceComplexity.explanation: No auxiliary memory allocated; uses only two integer index variables.

edgeCases: Array with exactly two elements: must check both.

approaches.name: Approach 2: Sort + Two Pointers
approaches.intuition: If the array was sorted, we could use two pointers starting from opposite ends and narrow the window based on whether the sum is too small or too large. However, since the question asks for original indices, we must pair each value with its original index before sorting.
approaches.theory: When sorted, if `nums[left] + nums[right] < target`, the only way to increase the sum is to increment `left`. Conversely, if the sum > target, decrement `right`. This reduces the search phase to O(N) after an O(N log N) sort.

timeComplexity.explanation: Sorting N pairs dominates the linear two-pointer scan.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Allocates a vector of pairs to preserve original indices.

edgeCases: Integer overflow when adding two large numbers: cast to `long long`.

approaches.name: Approach 3: One-Pass Hash Map (Optimal)
approaches.intuition: For each number `x`, we require its complement `target - x`. Instead of scanning backwards repeatedly, we store seen numbers in an unordered hash map. In a single pass, if `complement` is already in the map, we have found our answer in O(1) average lookup time.
approaches.theory: By trading space for time, a hash table provides expected O(1) amortized insertion and lookup via hashing. As we iterate left to right, every previous element has been indexed, ensuring no element pairs with itself and duplicate values are handled naturally.

timeComplexity.explanation: Traverses the array of size N exactly once. Hash map find and insert operations take O(1) amortized time.

spaceComplexity.explanation: In the worst case, stores up to N elements in the unordered_map.

steps: i=0: num=2, complement=7. Not in map. Map: {2: 0}
i=1: num=11, complement=-2. Not in map. Map: {2: 0, 11: 1}
i=2: num=7, complement=2. Found in map! Index: 0.

edgeCases: Duplicate elements that add up to target (e.g. nums=[3, 3], target=6): when the second 3 is processed, complement 3 is already in the map, returning [0, 1] before collision overwrites.
